title: Cass Sunstein on informational standing after Akins
shortTitle: Cass Sunstein on informational standing after Akins
summary: Sunstein reads Akins as supporting substantial congressional power to create enforceable interests; the casebook contrasts that theory with later concrete-injury decisions.
notes:
The assigned excerpt from Informational Regulation and Informational Standing: Akins and Beyond first acknowledges a narrow reading: Akins might protect informational injury especially because it directly serves voting. Sunstein then argues for a broader account in which the law substantially defines which interests count as injury. If Congress may create rights to information, he asks why it cannot create interests in preservation of species, pristine land, clean air, or other public goods.

His examples explore whether Congress could create property-like interests even for citizens who never visit a particular environmental site. The argument emphasizes legislative choice, the value people assign to a resource’s existence, and statutory design capable of creating novel enforceable interests. These are scholarly proposals and interpretations, rather than holdings that all such statutes would be constitutional.

The editors follow the excerpt with FECA decisions applying informational standing and then with TransUnion’s insistence on independently concrete harm. Raines also shows that explicit congressional authorization is not always sufficient. Reading those materials together preserves the live disagreement over how much freedom Congress has to define the injury that permits federal adjudication.
